title: "Expanded evidence extraction: preoperative pathology evaluation in prolapse"
format:
  docx:
    toc: true
execute:
  echo: false
---

This extraction supports preliminary model calibration; it is not a
procedure-specific comparative effectiveness estimate. The target population
is asymptomatic postmenopausal women with stage III uterovaginal prolapse.
Published mixed-population studies are labeled as indirect.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-expanded-evidence
#| tbl-cap: "Source-level evidence, including numerator/denominator and applicability"
source_rows <- readr::read_csv(
  "evidence/expanded_screening_extraction_20261109.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
display_rows <- source_rows |>
  dplyr::filter(evidence_class != "missing") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Count = dplyr::if_else(
      !is.na(numerator) & !is.na(denominator),
      paste0(numerator, "/", denominator),
      "—"
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    procedure_group, parameter, Count, published_estimate,
    evidence_class, limitations
  )
knitr::kable(display_rows)
```

## Highest-priority unobserved parameters

```{r}
#| label: tbl-critical-gaps
#| tbl-cap: "Missing inputs for decision modeling"
source_rows |>
  dplyr::filter(evidence_class == "missing") |>
  dplyr::select(procedure_group, parameter, limitations) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Rules for using these data

- Use 1/317 for the observed EIN proportion in the asymptomatic
  postmenopausal cohort; do not substitute the 2/106 rate of *combined*
  premalignant/malignant pathology *among patients with polyps*.
- The 8/462 complex atypical hyperplasia estimate comes from a broader POP
  hysterectomy series and is not restricted to postmenopausal patients in the
  reported denominator.
- The 10/30 second-staging estimate is conditional on incidental endometrial
  cancer. Do not apply it to the general prolapse population.
- A 38% complication estimate among selected *inpatient* trachelectomies after SCH does
  not estimate the probability of complications after SCH itself.
- Future cervix surveillance needs screening eligibility, prior CIN2+/AIS,
  age, and time horizon; screening is not automatically lifelong.
- Keep incident cancer after hysteropexy separate from occult cancer present
  at the index operation; the current model only represents prevalent disease.
- Test performance borrowed from patients with postmenopausal bleeding
  should be sensitivity analyses until validated for asymptomatic patients.
- Do not infer the causal value of earlier detection from survival comparisons
  of patients whose cancer was found before versus after prolapse surgery.

## Interpretation

Current evidence can justify broad sensitivity distributions for occult
endometrial cancer and can inform conditional second-staging probabilities
following unexpected cancer. It is not sufficient to estimate the effect of
routine testing on cancer mortality, the absolute post-hysteropexy diagnostic
delay, or the absolute probability of trachelectomy after SCH.
Those missing quantities should remain explicit scenario parameters.

The source URLs and study-specific limitations are retained in the linked CSV
for audit and future manuscript references.


## SCH with mesh sacrocolpopexy: unexpected endometrial pathology

In a retrospective single-center series of 226 sacrocolpopexies with
concomitant supracervical hysterectomy, histopathology identified atypical
endometrial hyperplasia in 14/226 (6.2%) and endometrial carcinoma in 1/226
(0.4%). All 15 patients had reportedly undergone preoperative pelvic
ultrasound and cervical cytology without suspicious findings. These tests
cannot be interpreted as validated endometrial screening with negative
predictive value in asymptomatic women. The 6.2% atypia estimate is much
higher than other prolapse cohorts; it is a heterogeneity signal and **not**
a default EIN prevalence parameter. [6]

### Management observed in the case series

Two patients with focal atypia whose specimens underwent uncontained power
morcellation received progestin therapy and clinical/ultrasound surveillance,
without immediate reoperation. The 80-year-old patient with a stage I
endometrial carcinoma underwent imaging assessment and surveillance instead
of trachelectomy after individualized multidisciplinary evaluation. The
article did not report immediate trachelectomy among these cases. No
oncologic recurrence was reported over a mean 26-month follow-up among
patients with endometrial lesions. This small, selected series and limited
follow-up do **not** establish that surveillance is oncologically equivalent
to completion surgery. [6]

For decision modeling, unexpected atypia/cancer after SCH must branch into:
(i) further assessment and surveillance, (ii) medical treatment and
surveillance, and (iii) additional surgery when indicated, potentially
including trachelectomy and oncologic staging. Assign no observed
branch probabilities from this small series: the untreated and treated
subgroups are not exchangeable, and the published description does not
establish a complete management denominator for every branch. Trachelectomy
is **not automatic** after unexpected endometrial pathology; equally, its
absence in this series is **not** evidence that it is never appropriate.

Known EIN/atypical endometrial hyperplasia should be managed according
to established guidance: ACOG identifies total hysterectomy as definitive
treatment, advises against supracervical hysterectomy as treatment for EIN,
and recommends progestin with histologic surveillance when surgery is
not an option. [7] The present study concerns *unexpected* pathology after
an SCH already performed, not planned surgery for known EIN.

6. Occult endometrial pathologies diagnosed after sacrocolpopexy with
   concomitant supracervical hysterectomy for pelvic organ prolapse.
   *Frontiers in Surgery*. 2026.
   https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12907406/
7. ACOG Clinical Consensus No. 5. Management of Endometrial
   Intraepithelial Neoplasia or Atypical Endometrial Hyperplasia. 2023.
   https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2023/09/management-of-endometrial-intraepithelial-neoplasia-or-atypical-endometrial-hyperplasia


## Newly extracted hysteropexy follow-up evidence

Two cohorts give direct, but incomplete, evidence for the consequences of
uterus preservation:

- Kurian et al. (2021) identified **0 confirmed subsequent primary uterine
  or cervical cancers among 755 hysteropexy patients** in an EHR cohort,
  with median follow-up of **1,480 days**. The largest reported 95% CI upper
  bound was **0.61%**. Cases of malignancy known at index surgery were
  excluded. This is neither an occult-pathology prevalence estimate nor
  evidence of no lifetime risk. Source:
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33620910/
- A multicenter cohort included **147 sacrospinous and 114 uterosacral
  hysteropexies**. With median follow-up of **17 months**, **4.6%** underwent
  subsequent hysterectomy and **6.5%** received treatment for uterine or
  cervical pathology. Only **83/261 (32%)** had one-year follow-up. The
  percentages are **not** rates of subsequent cancer, nor probabilities of
  hysterectomy preventable by preoperative screening. Source:
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36516026/

## New risk-factor evidence specific to SCH and SCP

In the 2026 SCH/SCP cohort, all 15 patients with unexpected atypia/cancer
were postmenopausal; mean age was 66.3 versus 59.1 years (p=0.03).
Tamoxifen exposure was reported in 13.3% versus 1.9% (p=0.05), and
hypertension in 53.3% versus 23.7% (p=0.017), comparing lesion to
nonlesion groups. These **unadjusted, sparse associations** do not define
a validated risk score and should not be converted into independent
multiplicative risk ratios. Source:
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12907406/

### Consequence for calibration

The **risk-stratified model must remain uncalibrated** until investigators
can estimate disease prevalence within explicitly defined average-risk and
elevated-risk subgroups, and the fraction of the target population falling
in each subgroup. No published risk model of **future incident** cancer
should be used as a proxy for prevalent occult pathology at surgery.
Separately estimate benign subsequent hysterectomy, pathological
surveillance/treatment, and cancer-specific management after hysteropexy.

## Additional evidence search: occult findings and risk triage

- A vaginal-hysterectomy-for-POP cohort reported **0.35%**
  significant endometrial pathology among *asymptomatic postmenopausal*
  patients despite an unremarkable preoperative workup. This is
  the residual pathology after a particular workup, not the untested
  disease prevalence or a validated screening false-negative rate.
  Full-text subgroup counts and workup definitions remain necessary.
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29103241/
- Among 569 vaginal hysterectomies with pelvic floor repair, **2/569**
  had unexpected endometrial cancer and **6/569** had unexpected
  premalignant uterine pathology. Abnormal endometrial findings on
  preoperative ultrasound were associated with unexpected malignancy
  (reported OR **4.63**, 95% CI **1.84–51.4**); age, BMI and POP-Q
  stage were not significantly associated. Because there were only
  two cancers, the association is highly uncertain and the endpoint
  requires full-text verification. It cannot be used directly as a
  two-stratum prevalence ratio.
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37401960/
- A 2010 prolapse study reported **2.6%** unanticipated uterine
  pathology among postmenopausal women without bleeding, but this
  encompassed premalignant and other pathology, not EIN or cancer
  alone. Full-text subgroup counts are needed.
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20452498/
- A Belgian 2024 conference abstract reports **19/235** lesions after
  sacrocolpopexy and hysterectomy. It appears to overlap the later
  Belgian 226-patient SCH/SCP report in institution and recruitment
  period. **Do not count it as an independent cohort** in prevalence
  meta-analysis until investigators confirm whether cohorts overlap.
  https://www.esgecongress.eu/files/inhalt/esge-2024/downloads/OFFICIAL_ABSTRACT_PUBLICATION_2024_v2.pdf

**Current interpretation:** These studies strengthen the rationale for
testing ultrasound-triggered risk triage as a *scenario* but do not
calibrate the elevated-risk group's absolute prevalence. The
screening policy model remains uncalibrated; no procedure-specific
screening recommendation or causal benefit should be inferred.

## 2026 additional cohort: occult cancer despite preoperative evaluation

Li and colleagues analyzed **3,588 hysterectomies during pelvic organ
prolapse repair** at a Chinese tertiary center. **Eleven** patients
(11/3,588, **0.31%**) had unexpected endometrial malignancy without
preoperative symptoms or suspicious ancillary findings. Ten were
endometrioid and one was serous carcinoma. **Seven of eleven (63.6%)**
underwent a second staging operation. The 0.31% pertains to residual
unexpected disease *after the institution's assessment practices*, not
occult cancer prevalence in an unscreened population.
https://gocm-frontend.bmj.com/content/6/2/e000221

The authors propose elevated BMI and metabolic comorbidities to identify
candidates for biopsy or hysteroscopy. Because the paper characterizes the
**eleven cancer cases** rather than applying the rule to every woman
without cancer, the source does **not** supply specificity, the fraction
screened, positive predictive value or stratum-specific absolute risks.
The paper's proposed rule and stated case capture should be verified
against the supplementary case table before using it even as a scenario.
The BMI cutoffs are defined using Chinese criteria and require local
transport validation.

The 7/11 staging estimate is another **conditional** rate, independent of
a US cohort with 10/30 staging. Their different case mixes and treatment
settings prohibit casual pooling without a prespecified heterogeneity
analysis.

## 2026 concurrent carcinoma in diagnosed atypical hyperplasia

A separate retrospective study of **101 women with preoperatively
diagnosed atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH)** found **37 (36.6%)**
with coexisting carcinoma on hysterectomy pathology. This is relevant
*after a positive biopsy* for counseling and management, but cannot be
used as EIN prevalence in unselected prolapse patients or as a screening
test sensitivity.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41611996/

**Research priority:** Extract full denominators for a candidate risk
rule among both cancer and non-cancer prolapse patients. Without them,
the risk-stratified model's tested fraction, specificity, and prevalence
remain uncalibrated.
